subtitle: Code-switching involves changes in self-presentation. Examine those changes, the pressure behind them and the actual communication task, without assigning one proper way to belong.
scope: For staff across DHS. Original workplace and private learning cases distinguish linguistic code-switching from broader changes in self-presentation discussed in workplace inclusion. A reported experience is not a group profile, a diagnosis, an individual IDI placement or a completed legal finding. Actual task, policy and assigned role responsibilities remain. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA. Participation in this learning is voluntary.
introTranscript: Kira describes changing how she opens a workplace explanation because she worries that familiar expressions will count against her. A colleague’s different choice does not erase that account. Examine the actual content, hear two personally learned meanings and consider a response that respects choice while questioning an unsupported style judgment. Use the full example or private unrecorded reflection; no personal performance or workplace disclosure is required.

intro.heading: Understand the term without guessing the person’s purpose
intro.body:
Kira is an adult in an original practice workplace case. She identifies herself as Black and says she has begun replacing a familiar greeting, hey folks, with good morning everyone when presenting an explanation. She says she worries that her usual expressions will be dismissed as unprofessional. No audio recording, measured speech difference, performance result or conclusion about a policy violation is supplied. The account concerns her stated experience, not every Black employee’s experience.

Code-switching has more than one use. In linguistics it concerns switching between languages or dialects within an interaction. Workplace inclusion discussions also use the term more broadly for changes in speech, expression, behavior or appearance associated with expectations about fitting an accepted norm. The SAEM authors distinguish these uses in their medical education resource. McCluney’s eCornell event overview addresses workplace cultural norms and pressure experienced by marginalized people. Those contexts help frame questions here; they do not provide an individual assessment of Kira or a new DHS rule.

Kira’s two greetings do not by themselves demonstrate switching between languages or dialects. It would be inaccurate to label the supplied wording as proof of a specific linguistic process. Her own explanation does make the broader self-presentation question relevant: she is considering how an accepted workplace style may affect how others judge her. That is different from assuming that every ordinary change in greeting is imposed, harmful or culturally informed adaptation.

Ellis, a colleague, initially says that everyone changes their wording, so there is nothing to consider. Changing language across contexts is possible, but that observation does not answer Kira’s particular concern about acceptance. It also does not establish that her explanation was clear, unclear, selected or rejected. The next lessons supply a concrete communication task and another person’s distinct choice rather than treating a general statement as an answer to all those questions.

Privately separate the observed or reported adjustment, the reason Kira supplies and the conclusions Ellis adds. You may reflect unrecorded on an expression that carries meaning in your own life, without identifying a protected class, recounting a harmful incident or proving a public version of authenticity. The full example supports every activity.

flashcards.back: Using different languages or dialects within an interaction; it is not automatically evidence of confusion or inability.
How someone presents speech, expression or appearance in a particular setting.
A perceived or stated expectation to resemble an accepted style, distinct from a demonstrated task requirement.
An adjustment a person describes as useful or preferred, without assuming everyone experiences the same freedom or cost.
The actual information or exchange that needs attention, rather than an undefined demand to sound like somebody else.
Understanding a personally learned expression or pressure without having to disclose it or perform a supposedly authentic self.

items.title: Keep the meaning of the term clear
items.body: The linguistic use asks about languages or dialects within an exchange. The workplace use can ask about self-presentation and acceptance. Kira’s supplied two greetings do not establish dialect switching; her reported worry does support examining the second question. Keeping them distinct prevents a term from becoming a diagnosis or language-ability judgment.

items.title: Hear the personally supplied reason
items.body: Kira links the change to concern about being judged. An observer who notices different wording but has not heard that reason has less information. Even with the account, the observer does not know every effect, workplace decision or policy finding. Listening adds a relevant perspective without supplying those missing results.

items.title: Leave the whole person open
items.body: A greeting does not establish Kira’s complete cultural identity or a permanent level of development. A person can choose different expressions and remain connected to several meanings. The course does not require one preferred expression to be displayed publicly so that another person can decide whether she is authentic.

tabs.label: One changed greeting proves a language deficit
tabs.body: Ellis treats different wording as confusion or inability. The example contains no language task result or qualification assessment, and the two greetings do not establish dialect switching. This explanation adds an ability judgment rather than examining the stated concern.

tabs.label: Everyone adjusts, so the concern disappears
tabs.body: Ellis points to common contextual changes and concludes that Kira’s worry needs no attention. Similar outward changes can have different reasons and costs. The general observation does not refute Kira’s particular account or examine the workplace expectation she is describing.

tabs.label: The term and actual account stay together
tabs.body: Ellis distinguishes the linguistic question from workplace self-presentation and hears the reason Kira supplies. Actual content, decisions and effects remain separate. This makes a more specific inquiry possible without assigning a group trait, a total identity or an individual IDI position.

check.question: Which account fits the example?
check.correct: Kira reports a self-presentation change linked to acceptance concerns; the two greetings alone do not establish dialect switching, ability or an actual workplace outcome.
wrong: The change proves that Kira cannot communicate a clear explanation.
Any changed greeting is necessarily a harmful act imposed by a workplace.
Because people often adjust wording, Kira’s stated concern has no relevance.
check.feedbackCorrect: This retains the actual term distinction and account without inventing a capability, universal cause or result.
check.feedbackIncorrect: No communication performance result establishes inability. A greeting change alone cannot show imposition or harm in every case. A common adjustment does not cancel Kira’s supplied concern; the reason and actual task still need attention.

A change can have a personally supplied purpose rather than a guessed motive.
Every change reveals deficient language ability.
The greeting establishes Kira’s complete identity and orientation.

Identify what either account can and cannot establish about other people.
Explain why self-understanding can matter without an imposed public performance.
takeaways: A similar adjustment can carry a different purpose.
One person’s preference does not refute another person’s reported pressure.

lessons.statement: Hear each person’s account rather than making either experience the rule for everyone.

image.caption: People sit around a table with laptops while another person points to a whiteboard.

intro.heading: Distinguish choice from a pressure another person describes
intro.body:
Devon, another adult in the example, says he prefers a brief greeting before a detailed explanation because it helps him enter the task without a personal opening. He does not say that Kira should follow his choice or that everyone is equally comfortable making it. Kira says that her own concern is different: she is checking how her expression will be judged, not simply deciding how much personal information to offer. These are two stated accounts, not competing measurements of who is truly comfortable.

An observer could wrongly use Devon’s preference to erase Kira’s concern. Another could use Kira’s concern to insist that Devon must secretly be under the same pressure. Both replace what the adults have supplied. A particular adjustment can be chosen for usefulness, privacy or enjoyment; another can be linked to anticipated judgment. The course does not decide that the visible change alone reveals the reason. Nor does it assume that choice and pressure are perfectly separate in every real experience. A person may have mixed reasons and may not want to explain them.

Ellis wants to help and proposes that Kira prove confidence by using her usual expression at the next explanation. That proposal can become a new demand. It makes Kira responsible for a public demonstration of authenticity and assumes Ellis can decide which version of her is genuine. Kira has not accepted that assignment. She may choose either greeting, another expression or a private conversation about the expectation without owing a performance.

Respecting her choice does not mean treating the workplace question as settled. Ellis can hear the concern and examine the specific judgment or proposed criterion through the appropriate responsibilities. At this point the example does not tell us an actual selection decision, completed inquiry or workplace remedy. The course values the clearer distinction between preference and pressure while those results remain open.

Use the full example, or privately consider an expression you have chosen and a context in which the choice felt narrower. You need not name a protected class, identify a colleague, recreate a harmful exchange or submit notes. A better understanding of your own choices can be meaningful without a changed workplace product. It should not become a personal score or an instruction to change how somebody else presents themselves.

lessons.keyStatement: Hear each person’s account rather than making either experience the rule for everyone.

items.title: The accounts are not interchangeable
items.body: Devon describes a useful private opening; Kira describes worry about acceptance. If Ellis uses one as proof against the other, a difference in experience disappears. Holding both accounts helps examine the context without deciding what all people with a similar identity must feel.

items.title: Choice can remain with the person
items.body: Kira has not agreed to a performance of confidence. Requiring a usual greeting may look supportive but still assigns her a way to be authentic. A more fitting response can acknowledge the concern and leave her next expression with her, alongside the actual communication task and relevant responsibilities.

items.title: A mixed account need not be forced into a score
items.body: A person could enjoy an adjustment and also experience pressure. Someone else may not want to explain. The learning can recognize that possibility without measuring a hidden motive or asking for proof. The example already gives enough information to compare the stated experiences.

tabs.label: Devon’s preference disproves Kira’s concern
tabs.body: Ellis concludes that because Devon likes a brief greeting, Kira has misunderstood her experience. Preference in one account does not establish freedom or cost in another. This approach avoids the context by making one adult’s explanation the answer for both.

tabs.label: Kira must demonstrate a genuine self
tabs.body: Ellis insists on a public familiar greeting as evidence that Kira is confident and authentic. That adds a performance requirement she has not chosen and gives Ellis authority over her identity. Supporting a choice differs from prescribing which expression proves it.

tabs.label: Both accounts inform a specific response
tabs.body: Ellis hears the two different purposes and leaves the adults’ self-presentation choices intact. A reported workplace expectation can still be examined without treating Devon as a counterexample or Kira as a public demonstration. Clearer private understanding is worthwhile while actual outcomes remain open.

check.question: Which comparison preserves the two adults’ accounts?
check.correct: Devon describes a preferred private opening; Kira describes concern about acceptance. Neither supplies the reason for every person’s adjustment or requires a public authentic-self performance.
wrong: Devon’s preference proves that Kira has no reason to consider workplace pressure.
Kira’s account proves that Devon must be hiding the same concern.
Kira must use her usual greeting publicly before her concern can be taken seriously.
check.feedbackCorrect: This compares the actual reasons while keeping choice and the limits of each account visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Devon’s preference does not establish Kira’s experience. Kira’s concern cannot reveal Devon’s hidden reason. A compulsory performance is an invented prerequisite, not evidence necessary for a voluntary account or the appropriate response to an actual concern.

items.text: Devon prefers a brief opening that leaves personal information private.
Kira worries about judgment of a familiar expression.
Hear the concern without prescribing the next greeting.
Privately examine mixed reasons using the full example.
Devon must secretly feel exactly what Kira feels.
Kira must prove authenticity through a public performance.

lessons.transfer: Privately explain how the two reasons differ and why neither adult owes a public performance.

move.control: You can distinguish your own purpose without demanding another person’s biography or expression.
move.failure: One account becomes everyone’s experience, or support becomes a compulsory display of authenticity.

lessons.statement: Understand the purpose another expression carries before treating your familiar style as the only serious one.

image.caption: People sit around a table with laptops while another person points to a whiteboard.

intro.heading: Let personally learned meanings widen the response
intro.body:
Kira offers another part of her account voluntarily. In a community kitchen she helped with, a playful greeting invited people to join a shared effort rather than stand apart from it. That experience made a warm opening meaningful to her. It did not make every playful expression suitable in every circumstance, and it does not describe what every Black person or kitchen participant prefers. Devon offers a different account: a mentor respected his ability to contribute without requiring a personal story, and a brief greeting still reminds him of that space.

Ellis initially hears Kira’s warmth as unserious and Devon’s brevity as distant. The meanings the people describe widen those interpretations. Warmth can communicate an invitation to shared work; brevity can preserve room for a chosen contribution. Neither account settles whether a particular explanation gives people what they need. Both do show why Ellis’s initial motive labels were too complete. The adults have meanings the people describe of their own rather than facts Ellis can infer from race, age, accent or an institution’s reputation.

Ellis considers a different opening for the practice explanation practice: each contributor may choose a short greeting, and everyone is invited to address the same actual information question in their own words. The proposal could welcome a warm entry without requiring a personal story and allow a brief entry without labeling it indifference. It is a proposal, not an adopted workplace rule or an agreement already supplied by the adults. Relevant actual responsibilities and communication requirements still need attention.

This is more than saying that styles differ. A specific personally learned purpose changes Ellis’s interpretation, and that wider interpretation changes what Ellis proposes. It is also different from asking Kira to be less recognizable or forcing Devon to become warmer for Ellis’s comfort. A culturally informed response needs the meaning and context; not every ordinary wording change automatically establishes official IDC Adaptation, and the course assigns no individual orientation.

You can privately reflect on a greeting, chosen expression or unspoken boundary that carries a learned meaning for you. The understanding can matter in its own right. You need not record the kitchen, mentor or personal connection, demonstrate it publicly or produce a work result. The full example provides the actual meanings needed for practice. Later agreement and experience of the proposed opening remain unknown.

lessons.keyStatement: Understand the purpose another expression carries before treating your familiar style as the only serious one.

items.title: Warmth can have a substantive purpose
items.body: Kira’s greeting connects to inviting people into a shared effort. Calling it unserious without that account misses the meaning she supplies. A wider frame can recognize the purpose and still examine whether the actual explanation answers the information question; welcome and content are connected but distinct.

items.title: Brevity can preserve room
items.body: Devon’s brief entry connects to contributing without a required story. Reading it as distance misses his stated experience of respect. A changed invitation can keep personal sharing optional rather than require Devon to display warmth in Ellis’s preferred way. It does not assume every brief speaker has Devon’s reason.

items.title: Make the proposal follow the meanings
items.body: Allowing chosen greetings and asking the shared information question connects the two purposes to a concrete exchange. It avoids reducing Kira’s account to fitting in or turning Devon’s privacy into failure. No acceptance or operational approval is supplied, so the learning should describe a fitting proposal rather than claim the next result.

tabs.label: Warmth means unseriousness; brevity means distance
tabs.body: Ellis keeps the original judgments and treats personal accounts as excuses. The supplied purposes challenge those labels: one invites shared effort, the other preserves chosen contribution. A style label does not answer the actual content question or describe the whole person.

tabs.label: Everyone must copy the same greeting
tabs.body: Ellis resolves the difference by prescribing one opening and removing all personal variation. That does not follow the two learned purposes and can recreate pressure to fit a single preferred style. Actual standards may have legitimate requirements, but none supplied here requires that universal greeting.

tabs.label: Chosen entry and shared content stay together
tabs.body: Ellis proposes room for a warm or brief greeting, with no personal story demanded, and turns attention to the information question. The response follows the actual meanings while maintaining the task. Acceptance, approval and effectiveness remain open rather than become automatic evidence of development.

check.question: Which proposal follows both personally meanings the people describe?
check.correct: Allow a chosen short greeting without a required personal story, then attend to the actual shared information question and relevant responsibilities.
wrong: Require Kira to be brief because warmth always prevents serious explanation.
Require Devon to offer a warm personal story to prove that he belongs.
Declare every ordinary change in greeting to be a completed IDC Adaptation assessment.
check.feedbackCorrect: This lets the wider interpretations change an exchange while preserving content, privacy and actual limits.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Kira’s warmth does not establish a content failure. Devon’s belonging need not be proved through disclosure or another person’s preferred expression. A greeting adjustment alone cannot establish a culturally informed developmental assessment; no individual orientation is assigned.

items.text: Kira connects warmth to joining a shared kitchen effort.
Devon connects brevity to room for chosen contribution.
Allow a short chosen greeting without a required story.
Ask the actual information question after the chosen opening.
Everyone sharing Kira’s identity must prefer playful openings.
The proposal proves an individual IDI orientation and acceptance.

lessons.transfer: Privately trace one original label, the supplied purpose that widens it and the different exchange it makes possible.

move.control: You can let a supplied meaning change your interpretation and proposal without assigning a person a stage.
move.failure: Personal meanings become group profiles, or a changed proposal becomes a developmental certificate.

intro.heading: Ask about the actual explanation rather than an undefined style ideal
intro.body:
The practice now supplies complete short explanations. Kira’s version begins, hey folks, and says that the page contains a worked example on the left and an open question on the right. Devon’s begins, good morning everyone, and supplies those same two facts. The invented page is a practice aid, not an actual service application, official hiring rubric or adopted agency document. In this example, a reader, Jules, asks whether the open question has already been answered. Neither supplied explanation states its answer status.

Ellis originally judged Devon’s greeting as more professional. That impression cannot establish that Devon answered Jules’s question better than Kira. The supplied content is the same on the relevant point. Nor does the comparison prove that every expression always works for every task or audience. It gives a specific reason to distinguish a style preference from information that is actually present or missing in this practice.

A useful clarification would address whether the open question has an answer. The case does not yet supply that answer, so the course should not invent one. It would be equally inaccurate to announce that there are no unresolved concerns. Ellis can propose obtaining the actual status and explaining it clearly. Asking Kira to replace her greeting alone would leave Jules’s question unanswered. Requiring Devon to add playful language would also not supply the missing fact.

This distinction does not remove legitimate communication standards or authorize a learner to rewrite actual job requirements. In real work, the task, audience, relevant standards, evidence and authorized roles need attention. The practice comparison is not a new universal test or a decision about employment, language ability or legal discrimination. A specific concern about a reader’s understanding should be handled with the relevant information rather than converted into an identity verdict.

You may privately compare the two complete explanations and describe the missing fact without using a real colleague’s material. The clearer distinction can also help you understand how a familiar style has become persuasive to you. That personal insight is meaningful even if no workplace rule changes. Later clarification, reader understanding and any actual decision remain open.

items.title: Compare the relevant supplied content
items.body: Both invented explanations state where the worked example and open question appear. A preference for one greeting does not show a difference in those facts. This specific comparison can challenge Ellis’s shortcut without pretending that every format is equally effective in all circumstances.

items.title: Keep Jules’s question as a question
items.body: Jules asks whether an answer exists; neither explanation supplies the status. Treating that as proof of poor ability or approval invents a result. A relevant next inquiry concerns the actual answer status, and a response should retain uncertainty until that information is supplied.

items.title: Separate practice from actual authority
items.body: The practice comparison supplies no agency rubric, delegated selection power or service determination. A learner can examine the reasoning and keep actual duties with their authorized roles. The benefit is a more specific question, not an automatic rule against all communication standards or a new personnel score.

tabs.label: The preferred greeting proves better content
tabs.body: Ellis selects Devon’s explanation on style and declares Jules’s question answered. Both versions lack the answer status, so the conclusion adds a content result not supplied. The greeting cannot substitute for the missing information.

tabs.label: Changing the other greeting settles the gap
tabs.body: Ellis asks Kira to imitate Devon or Devon to imitate Kira and counts the revision as complete clarification. Either greeting change leaves the answer status unknown. This directs attention to self-presentation while the actual reader question stays unanswered.

tabs.label: Clarify the actual missing fact
tabs.body: Ellis distinguishes the shared content from the style impression and proposes obtaining the open question’s status. That can address the task without inventing performance, selection or comprehension. A future reply is still needed before the gap can be called resolved.

check.question: Which conclusion fits the supplied explanations and Jules’s question?
check.correct: Both explanations give the same two location facts and omit answer status; a relevant clarification concerns that missing information rather than a greeting-based ability verdict.
wrong: Devon’s greeting proves that Jules received an answer.
Kira must imitate Devon before the open question can have a status.
Because the versions share content, every future communication need and authorized standard is already satisfied.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps the content comparison specific and the unresolved fact visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Devon’s greeting does not supply answer status. Kira’s imitation cannot determine the missing fact. Shared content in this invented task does not settle every audience need, future result or actual authorized standard.

intro.heading: Keep actual workplace responsibilities alongside optional learning
intro.body:
In a separate practice DHS workplace case, manager Rowan receives an allegation that a colleague was denied an opportunity because of race and told to change race-related expression to be acceptable. The example describes an allegation, not a completed finding about what occurred, whether a rule was violated or which corrective action is appropriate. Rowan’s manager role matters. The course is not the agency’s investigation and cannot decide discipline.

MMB Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to immediately report all allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. They must follow their agency’s complaint and investigation procedures and/or Affirmative Action Plan. That immediate route cannot wait for a code-switching definition, proof of motive, a personal conversation, an apology, course completion or consultant review. Assigned procedures and authorized responsibilities remain, and retaliation is prohibited.

The policy’s duties are different from prescribing one reporting requirement to every person in every optional activity. Its employee and third-party provisions strongly encourage reporting through the specified routes; this case specifically supplies Rowan’s manager role and allegation. A learner’s private reflection is not made into an investigation file, and Kira’s voluntary account is not automatically converted into a completed finding. An actual report needs its actual context and procedures rather than a verdict borrowed from the earlier greeting comparison.

Actual DHS Equity responsibilities also remain. Employees incorporate an equity lens in their daily work and use the relevant toolkit. For actions with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for the policy’s specified approvals, the required formal analysis or scan and permitted customized arrangements retain their actual scope. The voluntary learning case does not automatically complete that work, create a new authorized instrument or confer decision power. Staff carry out their equity work; the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads this program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback without a new universal review gate.

Use the complete separate example to name Rowan’s immediate route and the finding not yet supplied. Personal learning can remain private and useful while actual duties proceed where applicable. Neither an unresolved allegation nor a choice to share less makes someone’s learning worthless. Participation in this learning is voluntary; a required actual responsibility is not made optional by that distinction.

items.title: Retain the immediate manager route
items.body: The separate case supplies Rowan’s manager role and a race-based allegation. The specified report goes immediately to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Requiring a definition test or conversation first would add a gate that does not belong to the duty; it also confuses optional learning with the actual response.

items.title: Keep report and finding separate
items.body: Reporting does not decide the allegation. Actual assigned complaint and investigation procedures govern relevant roles, and the course supplies no disciplinary finding. Rowan should not improvise a private inquiry outside those responsibilities or delay reporting, while any properly assigned role remains with its actual procedures.

items.title: Do the actual equity work through its appropriate scope
items.body: A reflection on style pressure can inform a relevant question, but it does not complete every analysis. Qualifying real actions use the applicable toolkit or permitted customized tool arrangements. Staff keep responsibility for the work, with consultant guidance rather than a new requirement that the consultant approve every review.

tabs.label: Require learning and proof first
tabs.body: Rowan waits for the colleague to demonstrate code-switching and prove motive before reporting. Those invented prerequisites delay the immediate manager duty. The actual allegation route does not depend on a course result or on a person demonstrating a supposedly authentic expression.

tabs.label: Let the example decide discipline and formal analysis
tabs.body: Rowan treats the greeting comparison as a completed investigation and required equity report. The practice supplies neither those findings nor the applicable analysis of an actual action. It cannot replace assigned procedures, evidence, roles or authority.

tabs.label: Keep the duties and learning distinct
tabs.body: Rowan immediately reports the allegation through the specified route and follows actual assigned procedures, with nonretaliation preserved. Optional learning can help examine assumptions without deciding the case. Actual formal analysis keeps its qualifying scope and appropriate tools.

intro.heading: Keep clearer understanding without inventing a workplace result
intro.body:
At the invented closing, Ellis says that Kira’s warmth can invite shared effort and Devon’s brevity can leave room for chosen contribution. Kira says she wants to consider how she opens the practice explanation without being assigned a public performance. Devon continues to prefer a brief opening. The proposed choice of greetings and shared information question has not been accepted as a workplace practice. Jules’s question about answer status still has no supplied reply. Rowan’s separate reporting duty remains actual, but the course supplies no report outcome or finding.

These accounts support a specific learning gain. Ellis has a wider frame for the two adults’ expressions rather than a total unserious or distant label. That frame supports a different proposal. It does not show that Ellis permanently changed every bias, that Kira feels no pressure, that Devon can speak for others or that every workplace requirement is now appropriate. A private learner may also better understand an expression, choice or pressure in their own life without sharing it.

A truthful continuation keeps the open parts visible. If the practice explanation proceeds, the actual answer status and Jules’s response would need their own information. If someone considers a real workplace practice, applicable standards, staff responsibilities and authorized decisions still matter. Kira’s choice should not be treated as a task to perform authenticity for Ellis, and Devon’s preference should not be treated as proof against Kira’s concern.

You can use the full example to revisit the original judgment, the supplied meaning that widened it and the changed proposal. You can also reflect unrecorded on your own way of speaking or choosing privacy. Neither path requires a workplace disclosure, public cultural display, personality score or imposed deadline. No universal follow-up event or personal reporting obligation is invented by the optional exercise.

Participation in this learning is voluntary. That learning status does not remove an actual duty in a supplied role. The aim is to understand self-presentation and pressure more carefully, preserve choice and attend to what the actual task needs, while later outcomes remain honest questions rather than reassuring claims.

lessons.keyStatement: Keep the particular gain, the person’s choice and the open results together.

items.title: Describe the selected gain
items.body: Ellis now connects the two greetings with shared effort and chosen contribution. That is a clearer account of the meanings the people describe and a reason for a different proposal. It is not a permanent competence score, a group profile or evidence that all pressure has disappeared.

items.title: Retain what has not happened
items.body: No workplace arrangement is supplied as accepted, Jules has no answer-status reply and the separate allegation has no finding. Counting those open matters as success or failure would add a result. A proposed next inquiry can be useful without claiming it has already occurred.

items.title: Keep choice and responsibility together
items.body: Kira can choose her expression without owing a demonstration, and Devon can keep a preferred brief entry. Their choices do not erase actual communication needs or Rowan’s duties. A private insight can be meaningful while real tasks and applicable procedures retain their own context and evidence.

tabs.label: Wider understanding proves complete resolution
tabs.body: Ellis declares that Kira has no remaining pressure and every reader understands the explanation. The supplied closing establishes neither. This turns an interpretation and proposal into results the course deliberately leaves open.

tabs.label: No workplace change means no worthwhile learning
tabs.body: Ellis dismisses the adults’ clearer purposes because no new practice has been adopted. That imposes an operational-result condition on private understanding and ignores the value of a less total judgment. A learning gain can matter alongside unresolved practical questions.

tabs.label: The gain and unknowns remain accurate
tabs.body: Ellis describes the wider meaning, a proposal and the actual missing answer status. Kira’s and Devon’s choices remain theirs, and the separate manager duty keeps its own route. This allows a proportionate continuation without inventing agreement, performance, legal findings or permanent change.

check.question: Which closing account fits the full example?
check.correct: Describe the wider meanings and proposal, retain the adults’ choices and keep acceptance, answer status and actual workplace outcomes open.
wrong: Ellis’s wider understanding proves that Kira has no remaining pressure.
Because no practice is adopted, private self-understanding cannot be worthwhile.
The optional exercise proves complete reader understanding and resolves the separate allegation.
check.feedbackCorrect: This values the specific gain while preserving choices and information the example has not supplied.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A wider interpretation does not reveal that Kira’s experience is fully resolved. Private understanding needs no adopted practice to have meaning. The exercise supplies neither Jules’s answer-status reply nor an allegation finding; actual responsibilities and outcomes remain distinct.

jobAid.title: Examine code-switching and workplace expectations
jobAid.subtitle: Hear the reason for a change, question a style shortcut and retain the actual communication task.
remember: Participation in this learning is voluntary.
Use the full example or private unrecorded reflection. No harmful-incident account, cultural performance, personal score or public authentic-self demonstration is required.
A reported experience is not every person’s experience. A proposal is not acceptance, a report is not a finding and a style impression is not task evidence.

sections.heading: Understand the question
items: Linguistic code-switching concerns different languages or dialects within an interaction. Broader workplace discussions can concern changes in self-presentation associated with accepted norms. Kira’s two greetings alone do not establish dialect switching.
Hear what changed and the reason the person chooses to supply. Do not infer language inability, total identity, motive or an individual IDI orientation from appearance or wording.

sections.heading: Distinguish preference and pressure
items: Devon prefers a brief opening; Kira reports concern about acceptance. One account does not refute the other, and neither supplies every person’s experience. Mixed reasons or a wish not to explain remain possible.
Supporting Kira does not require her to perform a usual expression publicly. Leave the next expression with the person rather than prescribe a supposedly authentic self.

sections.heading: Let meaning change the response
items: Kira’s warm greeting connects to inviting shared effort. Devon’s brief entry connects to room for chosen contribution. These personal accounts widen Ellis’s original unserious and distant labels without becoming group scripts.

A proposed chosen short greeting, optional story and shared information question follow both purposes. Acceptance and effectiveness remain open; not every greeting change proves official IDC Adaptation or a personal stage.

sections.heading: Examine the actual task
items: Both complete invented explanations locate the worked example on the left and the open question on the right. Neither supplies answer status. A preferred greeting does not establish better content or answer Jules’s question.

A relevant clarification concerns actual answer status. Real standards, audience needs and decision authority keep their appropriate scope; the practice comparison is not an adopted rubric, legal finding or personnel measure.

sections.heading: Keep actual responsibilities
items: In the separate manager case, Rowan immediately reports all protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follows actual complaint/investigation procedures and/or the agency Affirmative Action Plan. Proof, a conversation, apology, consultant review and learning completion cannot delay the duty.

Reporting is not a finding; assigned roles and nonretaliation remain. Employees and third parties are strongly encouraged to report through the policy’s specified routes; the case specifically supplies Rowan’s manager responsibility.

Actual DHS daily equity work and qualifying prolonged or long-term actions scheduled for specified approvals retain the applicable toolkit, formal analysis or scan and permitted customized arrangements. Staff do the work with Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leadership, guidance and feedback, without a new universal consultant gate. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.

sections.heading: Continue without inventing an outcome
items: Ellis’s wider understanding, Kira’s choice to consider an opening and Devon’s preference are supplied. Practice acceptance, Jules’s reply, all later workplace effects and the separate allegation result remain open.

A clearer private understanding can matter without a new practice or work product. Choose unrecorded reflection or an actual specific question through appropriate arrangements; unknown information remains unknown rather than proof of success, failure or no concerns.

sources.title: SAEM: Code Switching, by Mariame Fofana and Kari Haley
sources.note: Introduces linguistic and broader self-presentation uses in a medical-education context. The distinction informs careful questions; the DHS examples do not adopt medical scenarios, population figures or universal judgments about a person’s adjustments.

sources.title: eCornell: Codeswitching with Courtney L. McCluney
sources.note: Explores workplace cultural norms and pressures on marginalized people to change self-presentation. It provides context for the course questions, not a personal diagnosis, experiment result or new agency rule.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Supports inquiry into personally learned meanings, changing affiliations and a response informed by another perspective. Kira’s and Devon’s accounts are individual meanings rather than group profiles or inferred orientations.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Sets immediate manager/supervisor reporting of all protected-class allegations or incidents, assigned procedures and nonretaliation. An optional reflection or definition exercise cannot replace or delay the actual duty.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Explains daily equity responsibilities and the tools and roles for qualifying formal analysis. Comparing self-presentation in an example does not complete that work or grant authority.
